SLU and St. Louis community unites to resist potential cuts to African American, Women’s and Gender studies departments

Sam Bruemmer, Arts & Life Editor • November 9, 2026
The University News / Tanjid Rahman
Students, faculty and community members paint denim and share stories in the Pius Memorial Library on Nov. 5, 2026.
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:15
Instaread

The African American studies and women’s and gender studies departments, as well as the SLU community at large, have been pushing back against departmental reviews that were announced on Sept. 17 that may lead to undergraduate program cuts. 

The Strategic Implementation website states that the selection for departments for fiscal review followed the 2025 program Viability and Sustainability policy. The report details 11 guiding principles, one of which states that “good does not equal essential.”

“It is neither intellectually honest nor financially feasible for SLU to pursue every worthy academic curricular or scholarly endeavor – including all those reflecting our Jesuit educational heritage,” the policy states.

After the policy became public, the African American studies department invited students, faculty, alumni and community members to a town hall in Morrissey Hall on Nov. 2 to discuss the review and how the department planned to  move forward. The town hall included speeches, a panel of students and alumni and an open forum, with over 110 people in attendance.

The women’s and gender studies department held an event with a similar focus on Nov. 5 in Pius XII Memorial library. The event was centered around the importance of Title IX, featuring an activity that allowed participants to paint messages on denim. Attendees shared personal stories and experiences with misogyny, in addition to why they value the department.

Department leaders urged students to show support. Women’s and gender studies has a letter writing campaign and template emails for people to personalize and send. An anonymous student petition, as well as one sponsored by the African American studies department, have circulated and reached a combined total of over 3,000 signatures. One of the biggest asks was for students to simply enroll in the departments’ courses.

Both of these events were held in preparation for Tuesday, Nov. 10, where each department will be granted 20 minutes to present data to the Office of the Provost. Women’s and gender studies has planned to display the newly painted denim across the quad until 4 p.m., inviting passers-by to conversations about the reviews.

Following these events, the Office of the Provost sent a university-wide email about the reviews on Friday, Nov. 6, emphasizing that no outcomes are certain and shedding more light on the review process.

“Why are we conducting program reviews? One important goal is to strengthen SLU’s academic portfolio as a whole: ensuring academic programs are structured to support student success, academic quality and distinction, responsiveness to demand and emerging needs, and long-term sustainability,” the email read.

African American studies department:

 

Junior African American studies major CJ Summers said on the Nov. 2 panel that the review and its emphasis on budget echoed SLU’s treatment of Black people when it was first being built.

“What I hear when they say things like — that this is about money, that’s basically [the university] saying Black people is just dollar bills,” Summers said. “That is the same exact thing that this university was founded on, Black people being just dollar bills. So we see that the same cycle that was founded upon in 1818 is being repeated in 2026.”

Junior mechanical engineering major Isaiah Banks said SLU staff members may have discouraged participation in African American studies classes, which underscores the administration’s stated commitments to aligning program offerings with student interest. 

“A lot of the time, our academic advisers do not really tell us about these opportunities that we have. I’ve heard that they have steered students away from taking AFAM classes,” Banks said. “That is a structural issue. And I would like to say with my experience in AFAM, once I did find out about it … I felt a lot more like I belonged on campus, and I felt like I really created a family within the Black community at school, which I did not have before.”

St. Louis Alderwoman, SLU alum and Clock Tower Accords activist Alicia Sonnier said SLU’s partaking in slavery and urban renewal make African American studies necessary.

“In my opinion, if Saint Louis University is to dismantle or decline African American studies, you are doing something that’s to the antithesis of your mission,” Sonnier said. “Only so many groups’ literal blood, sweat and enslavement aided to the building of the institution. … Those are homes [at Mill Creek Valley]. Those are families. Those are people who had to literally be displaced out of their communities in order for the ivory tower to advance.

Women and gender studies department:

Women’s and gender studies professor and Denim Day organizer Alesha Durfee explained the importance of displaying denim and student artwork.

“When you see the total sum of the messages, it’s like a visual representation of how much women’s and gender studies, African American studies and American studies means to students and staff and the whole school community,” Durfee said.

Durfee said that review and potential program cuts could discount the hard work and long-term plans of students.

“When you talk about disestablishing a program or removing degree programs, this is something that students have been working towards their whole lives,” Durfee said. “I think our students deserve a display that is as visually impactful as removing these programs will be impactful in their lives, their careers, what they’ve worked for, what their families have worked for.”

Senior neuroscience and women’s and gender studies double major Shauna Prasad shared the practical benefits of the women’s and gender studies major.

“As I’ve been interviewing for medical schools, the first thing when they see me, they go, ‘you’re gonna graduate with a bachelor of arts in women and gender studies? That is so interesting. Please tell me more,’” Prasad said.

Sophomore neuroscience and women’s and gender studies major Amelia Webster echoed a similar sentiment to Isaiah Banks, explaining how another SLU faculty member made an offhand comment that she would have to complete women’s and gender studies courses elsewhere or disregard the credits she already earned.

Marlon Bailey, department chair of African American studies at Washington University in St. Louis, who also teaches courses in the women, gender and sexuality studies department, said that both areas of study emerge from protest movements.

“They offer creative ways of creating better futures, more equitable futures and ways to redress the harms done in the past,” Bailey said. “[This] society does not want students to learn how to, one, be critical of these systems that exclude us, and they don’t want us to be able to imagine alternative and better futures. … Fascist regimes always attack the university because that’s where the critical knowledge production happens.”

Webster said that the events and general response have inspired her to fight for the departments and raise her voice on their behalf.

“I think that it’s important that we put the pressure on and we should put these leaders in a hot seat,” Webster said. “I definitely just want to make it the biggest inconvenience possible for SLU to get rid of women’s and gender studies. … If they are going to take it away, they are going to have to pry it from my hands. And I’m gonna be so annoying and super terribly loud about it.”

About the Contributor
Sam Bruemmer, Arts & Life Co-Editor
Sam Bruemmer (he/they) is a sophomore from Bloomington, IL majoring in English and communication with a journalism concentration and minors in theater and creative writing. This is his second year editing for Arts & Life, and he loves writing everything from reviews to profiles to poetry and more. He also edits for the Kiln, plays in the drumline and concert band, plans events for the Rainbow Alliance and garners enough minutes listened on Spotify to scare his friends. You can spot him by his many stickers, keychains and bracelets (unless he’s off to work at the Fox Theater)!
